issues.legal_issue: A person who was not a party to a company winding-up proceeding may appeal an order that prejudicially affects that person’s rights.
material_facts: An order made in the company’s winding-up proceeding authorized the sale of leasehold rights said to have been created over land owned by a person who was not heard before the order was made.
That person appealed the order, but the High Court refused to entertain the appeal because she had not appeared before the Company Judge.
The High Court considered a suit after obtaining leave to be the person’s only remedy.
issues.conclusion: The appeal against the winding-up order was competent, and the High Court erred in refusing to entertain and decide it. The person could not be deprived of the appeal because she had not appeared when no notice had been given; a suit was not the only remedy.
issues.legal_principle: Section 483 of the Indian Companies Act, 1956 permits an appeal from an order or decision made in the matter of winding up, subject to the conditions applicable to appeals in ordinary jurisdiction. A non-party may appeal with leave where the order prejudicially affects that person, and leave should be granted in that circumstance. The failure to notify the affected person does not defeat the right to appeal. Section 446 does not make a suit after obtaining leave the exclusive remedy.

predicates.appeal_from_winding_up_order: A person seeks appellate review of an order made in a company winding-up proceeding.
predicates.appellant_not_a_party: The person seeking to appeal was not a party to the proceeding in which the order was made.
predicates.order_prejudicially_affects_appellant: The order prejudicially affects the appellant’s rights.

issues.definition: When a non-party seeks to appeal an order made in a company winding-up proceeding and that order prejudicially affects the non-party’s rights, leave to appeal should be granted.

issues.legal_issue: A court must give a person notice and a proper opportunity to be heard before making a winding-up direction that would prejudicially affect that person’s rights.
material_facts: The Official Liquidator sought directions to sell leasehold rights and structures on land owned by a person outside the winding-up proceeding.
The Company Judge ordered the sale without issuing notice to or hearing the landowner.
The sale order directly affected the landowner’s asserted rights in the land and leasehold rights.
issues.conclusion: The Official Liquidator and the Company Judge were required to notify and hear the person whose rights would be prejudicially affected before making the order.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 103 of the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959 provides for summons seeking directions concerning, among other matters, the Official Liquidator’s exercise of powers under section 457(1) of the Indian Companies Act, 1956, including the power to sell company property. Although the Rule expressly requires notice to the winding-up petitioner, it implicitly requires notice to any person who would be prejudicially affected by the directions. Natural justice requires notice and a proper opportunity to present that person’s case before an order affecting the person’s rights is made. Rule 139 did not justify denying the appeal because the affected person had not appeared before the Company Judge.

predicates.winding_up_court_direction: A court considers a request for directions in a company winding-up proceeding.
predicates.direction_prejudicially_affects_nonparty: The proposed direction would prejudicially affect the rights of a person who is not a party to the proceeding.
predicates.nonparty_not_given_notice_or_hearing: The affected non-party has not been notified of the request or given an opportunity to present their case.

issues.definition: If a court considers a winding-up direction that would prejudicially affect a non-party who has not received notice or an opportunity to be heard, notice and an opportunity to be heard are required.
